Adding a conv on a previously removed edge contributes new capacity and a new path, unlike replacing an existing pool or 1x1 op (exp 1-2 vs 3-4, 7).

Without the residual edge, adding a conv path from node 1 to the output matters much more for gradient flow and capacity (exp 100 vs 91-96).
When edge 1 is already absent, removing edge 0 disconnects nodes 1 and 2 from the input and collapses the cell (exp 27,28 vs others).
Without the input-to-output skip, cutting edge 0 can leave the output with no path to the input, which is catastrophic (exp 27).
If node 2 has no outgoing edge, adding a conv into node 2 is a dead end that cannot reach the output (exp 52,54,56,58 vs paired 51,53,55,57).
With edge 5 removed, computation flowing into node 2 never reaches the output, so upgrading edge 2 is wasted (exp 32,36,38 vs 31,35,37).
In parameter-free, pool-dominated cells the residual skip lets the identity overwhelm the weak signal and sharply hurts accuracy (exp 15,16).
